title: Power Law Amplitude Estimation for Option Pricing with NISQ Devices
abstract_summary: The paper proposes applying a power law amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm to option pricing on NISQ devices, aiming to reduce circuit depth compared with standard AE and QFT-free approaches. The authors present a quantum circuit that loads log-normal asset distributions and encodes European call payoffs, analyze estimation performance via Fisher information, and report Qiskit simulations showing an overall accuracy improvement of about 13.12% over other AE methods.
methodology_description: The paper proposes and evaluates a power-law amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm for pricing European call options on NISQ devices. The methodology composes a quantum operator F_pl = R (G ⊗ I) where G loads a discretized probability distribution of the underlying asset prices into an n-qubit register (amplitudes proportional to probabilities) and R encodes a piecewise-linear payoff onto an ancilla qubit via a comparator (flag) and controlled Ry rotations. The ancilla measurement probability P_pl is related analytically to the expected payoff E[g(V)] up to a known affine scaling, allowing recovery of the option price. The algorithm uses a Grover-like operator F_pl and a power-law schedule of amplification depths q_k (q_k as given in the paper) with a fixed number of shots per schedule step N_shot. For each schedule element k the ancilla is measured N_shot times, producing counts N1_k and N0_k; the likelihood over θ_pl (where P_pl = sin^2 θ_pl) is accumulated across k (Equation (15)) and a Bayesian/maximum-likelihood classical post-processing step finds the θ_pl that maximizes the posterior (Equation (16)). Fisher information is used to analyze scaling and to choose parameters M (number of schedule steps) and 𝛽. The methodology is validated by numerical simulation on Qiskit: (a) constructing explicit small circuits (three qubits: two for asset register, one ancilla) that implement distribution loading (CNOT and Ry gates) and the payoff (comparison + controlled Ry); (b) running power-law AE with different schedule parameters (k, 𝛽) and comparing against a QFT-free AE baseline (exponential schedule q_k = 2^k) and the analytical Black–Scholes–Merton price. Performance is reported in terms of estimated option price accuracy and number of oracle calls vs target error 𝜀.
experimental_setup: Numerical simulation on Qiskit. Circuits use 3 qubits (2 asset register qubits + 1 ancilla). Asset terminal price distribution is a truncated log-normal (Black–Scholes–Merton) discretized into 4 states (2 qubits). Strike price K = 6.00. Scaling factor for payoff encoding set to ~0.25. Power-law scheduling experiments used k in {3,5,7,9} and 𝛽 values {0.417, 0.625}; QFT-free AE used exponential schedule q_k = 2^k as baseline. Exact Qiskit backend not specified.
dataset_used: Synthetic financial dataset: terminal asset price distribution following a log-normal distribution per the Black–Scholes–Merton model (parameters: volatility 50%, risk-free rate 2%, spot price 7, T = 30/365). The continuous distribution is truncated to ±3 standard deviations and discretized into 2 qubits (4 price bins) with resulting prices [3.981, 6.001, 8.022, 10.042] and probabilities [0.1%, 55.9%, 42.0%, 2.0%].

experiment_input.preprocessing: Truncate continuous log-normal to ±3σ, discretize into 2^n = 4 bins (mapped to computational basis states of 2 qubits), scale payoff angles by a chosen factor (≈0.25). Encode probabilities as amplitudes using CNOT + Ry rotations as shown in the 2-qubit loading circuit.

steps: Discretize and truncate the log-normal terminal price distribution and map bins to n-qubit basis states.
Construct quantum loading circuit G (CNOT and Ry gates) to prepare |φ> = Σ sqrt(p_i) |i> on the asset register.
Attach an ancilla initialized and rotated to angle (π/4 - c); perform a quantum comparator to set a flag qubit for i >= K.
Apply controlled Ry rotations on the ancilla conditioned on the flag and asset index to encode payoff via angle ˜g(i) = 2c(i - K)/(2^n - 1 - K).
Define the overall operator F_pl and Grover-like operator 𝓕_pl = -F_pl R_0 F_pl^† R_pl.
Schedule repetitions q_k according to the power-law schedule q_k = floor(k^{(1−β)/(2β)}) (as presented) with k = 1..M and constant number of measurements N_shot per k.
For each k: apply 𝓕_pl q_k times, measure the ancilla N_shot times collecting counts N1_k and N0_k.
Form the likelihood across k (Equation (15)) and perform Bayesian updates / maximum-likelihood estimation to obtain θ_pl = argmax_θ ln ℒ(θ; {N1_k}).
Recover P_pl = sin^2 θ_pl and compute E[g(V)] from affine relation P_pl = 1/2 - c + (2c/(2^n - 1 - K)) E[g(V)].
Compare estimated option price to analytical Black–Scholes–Merton value and to QFT-free AE baseline; analyze number of oracle calls vs target error ε using Fisher information.
parameters_tuned: number of asset qubits n = 2 (4 bins)
c small parameter for ancilla rotation (not numerically specified)

reproducibility_notes: The paper states simulations were performed on Qiskit and provides circuit-level descriptions, numerical distribution parameters, and schedule/parameter choices (k values, β values, scaling). However, no code repository or exact Qiskit backend/shot counts are provided, and some implementation constants (e.g., exact c, exact N_shot) are not numerically specified. Reproduction is feasible in principle from the described circuits and parameter values but would require filling in unspecified numeric choices and implementing the likelihood/Bayesian inference procedure. Data sharing is reported as not applicable in the paper.
key_findings: [speculative] The paper proposes a power law amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm tailored for option pricing on NISQ devices that aims to reduce circuit depth compared with QFT-based AE.

[supported] The authors implement and simulate a three-qubit quantum circuit (two qubits for the asset distribution and one ancilla for payoff) in Qiskit for pricing a European call option under a discretized log-normal distribution.

[supported] In their Qiskit simulation benchmark the power law AE achieves an overall accuracy improvement of about 13.12% compared with the QFT-free AE scheduling for the tested instance (k up to 9).
[supported] The authors show (via simulation) that for loose target-error requirements the power law scheduling can approach optimal scheduling while keeping shallower circuit depth.

[speculative] The paper argues theoretically (and via Fisher information analysis) that the mean-squared estimation error lower bound scales as 1/I(y) and that under their setting the lower bound implies N_q = O(ε^{-1}).

[supported] The paper reports specific circuit and instance parameters used in simulation: discretized asset prices encoded on two qubits with values [3.981, 6.001, 8.022, 10.042] and corresponding probabilities [0.1%, 55.9%, 42.0%, 2.0%]; strike price K = 6.00; volatility = 50%; risk-free rate = 2%; spot price = 7; T = 30/365.

[speculative] They propose a scheduling family q_k = floor(k^{(1-β)/(2β)}) with β as a tuning parameter (examples β = 0.417 and β = 0.625) that balances oracle calls and circuit depth; they claim this puts performance between classical and optimal quantum scalings.

[supported] The paper verifies by simulation that exponential scheduling (q_k = 2^k) attains near-optimal quantum scaling for small target errors, whereas power-law scheduling retains shallower depth for practical (larger) error regimes.

[speculative] The authors claim the approach makes quantum amplitude estimation more NISQ-friendly and more practical for financial applications such as option pricing, portfolio optimization and risk assessment.
results_summary: The authors present a NISQ-oriented option-pricing approach that integrates a power law amplitude estimation schedule with a quantum circuit that loads a discretized log-normal asset distribution and encodes a European call payoff. They simulate the constructed three-qubit circuit in Qiskit for a representative instance and show that the power law AE scheduling can reduce circuit depth while improving overall estimation accuracy (reported ~13.12% improvement over a QFT-free AE scheduling instance). The paper includes a Fisher information-based analysis of estimation error scaling and empirical plots comparing scheduling strategies (power-law vs exponential), arguing that power-law scheduling offers a practical middle ground between classical and ideal quantum scalings for NISQ constraints.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper asserts quantum acceleration (quadratic speedup of amplitude estimation vs classical Monte Carlo) as background and argues that power-law AE brings this advantage closer to NISQ realizability by reducing circuit depth. The claim is supported by theory and Qiskit simulations on small instances, but not demonstrated on physical quantum hardware nor shown to provide practical advantage on large, realistic financial instances; therefore the advantage remains theoretical rather than experimentally demonstrated.
limitations: Execution of quantum AE algorithms is limited by the quantum depth available in current NISQ devices.
The QFT-free AE model reduces some overhead but does not fully eliminate depth limitations of quantum AE (author-stated).
Power-law AE shows slower convergence than QFT-free AE for small choices of k in the simulated examples (author-stated).
Power-law scheduling yields scaling between classical and optimal quantum; it does not achieve optimal quantum scaling for small target errors (author-stated).
The option-pricing model assumes the Black–Scholes–Merton (log-normal, constant volatility) framework, which limits applicability to more realistic market models.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Power-law amplitude estimation (AE) can achieve better accuracy (~13.12% improvement reported) than a QFT-free exponential-schedule AE baseline in simulated option-pricing instances.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — The power-law scheduling reduces required circuit depth relative to standard AE / QFT approaches and is presented as more NISQ-friendly.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical Bayesian/maximum-likelihood post-processing over measurement counts across schedule steps recovers the amplitude estimate (θ_pl) and the final option price.
#idea:quantum-advantage — Fisher information analysis is used to choose schedule parameters (M, β) and to characterize oracle-call scaling vs target error ε, suggesting improved resource trade-offs.
#limitation:simulation-only — Results are obtained via Qiskit numerical simulation on 3 qubits (2 asset qubits + 1 ancilla) with no experiments on real quantum hardware.
#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations use only 2 asset qubits (4 price bins) — the approach is not validated at realistic discretization scales required for production pricing.

#limitation:data-encoding — The protocol requires explicit amplitude-loading circuits and comparator-based piecewise-linear payoff encoding; the cost and scaling of loading larger, higher-resolution distributions is not empirically evaluated.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — While analytical relations and simulations are provided, claims about NISQ applicability and depth reduction are not validated on noisy hardware or large problem instances.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — The power-law schedule (q_k ~ floor(k^{(1-β)/(2β)})) offers a tunable trade-off between amplification depth and total measurements tailored for limited-depth devices.
